documents.abstract: The rapid expansion of digital technologies and artificial intelligence (AI) has transformed the landscape of science education by creating new opportunities for inquiry-based learning, virtual experimentation, and personalized instruction. Nevertheless, unequal access to digital devices, reliable internet connectivity, accessible learning resources, and digital literacy continues to limit equitable participation in science learning across India. This conceptual research paper examines digital access as the foundational condition for inclusive science education within the policy framework of the National Education Policy (NEP) 2020 and the national vision of Viksit Bharat 2047. Using a qualitative conceptual research design, the study synthesizes contemporary scholarly literature, UNESCO and OECD reports, NCERT publications, and Indian educational policy documents published between 2020 and 2026. The thematic analysis identifies five interconnected dimensions influencing inclusive science education: digital equity, virtual laboratories, AI-enabled pedagogy, teacher digital competence, and future-ready science learning. Based on this synthesis, the paper proposes an integrated conceptual framework demonstrating how equitable digital access supports competency-based science education through the interaction of infrastructure, pedagogy, technology, and teacher preparedness. The study argues that meaningful digital inclusion is not merely a technological objective but an educational imperative for achieving scientific literacy, social justice, and equitable learning opportunities in India.

Purpose This article documents the collaboration between a high school social studies teacher and a university professor – working within an existing school-university partnership – in the design and implementation of a geography-based Holocaust lesson to support authentic learning opportunities for preservice teachers. This article responds to calls for educators in school-university partnerships to tell stories of the creation, evolution, challenges and possibilities of boundary-spanning partnership work. Design/methodology/approach The article utilizes storytelling as a means of documenting the importance of relationships in partnership work. Because storytelling is not dependent on traditional methods and frameworks, the authors outline the background, challenges and successes around their planning, coordination and implementation of an original lesson plan developed to model best practices on teaching difficult histories in a safe environment. Findings As a storytelling account, this work does not present empirical or generalizable findings. The story is offered as an example to foster reflection and conversation within other school-university partnerships. Originality/value Our narrative, which captures how relationships are central to partnerships, provides an illustrative example of how partnerships can support efforts to address gaps in education research and in modeling for preservice teachers for how to teach difficult histories in high school social studies classes. The authors reflect on how trust, shared expertise, reciprocal learning and collaboration can support meaningful, relevant and boundary-spanning experiences within partnerships between high schools and universities and colleges.

Burnout syndrome is one of the leading occupational health problems currently affecting education professionals and represents a growing challenge to the quality and sustainability of educational systems. The objective of this article was to analyze burnout syndrome among teachers through a literature review of recent scientific evidence, examining its conceptual foundations, risk factors, consequences for well-being and professional performance, as well as the main prevention and intervention strategies. The literature search was conducted using international scientific databases and publications from specialized organizations, with priority given to studies published between 2018 and 2026. The reviewed evidence demonstrates that burnout is a multidimensional phenomenon arising from the interaction of high job demands, insufficient organizational support, administrative overload, limited opportunities for professional development, and work-life imbalance. Furthermore, the findings indicate that teacher burnout negatively affects mental health, job satisfaction, professional commitment, teaching quality, and educational outcomes. The studies analyzed consistently show that interventions focused exclusively on the individual are insufficient unless accompanied by structural changes within educational institutions. Consequently, burnout prevention requires comprehensive policies that combine the strengthening of personal resources with organizational strategies aimed at improving working conditions, promoting teacher well-being, and fostering higher-quality and more sustainable education.

Purpose This study aims to examine how Generative artificial intelligence (AI) based tools and technology supports skill development and capability enhancement for indigenous community-based tourism (CBT) practitioners. Emerging tools can serve as an ally in promoting sustainable income generation, economic empowerment and social inclusion for communities offering tourism services in remote locations. The study focuses on indigenous populations in Northeast India, a region renowned for its cultural and ethnic diversity but facing significant socio-economic challenges. Design/methodology/approach The researchers implemented a qualitative constructivist grounded theory method to collect data through literature reviews and interviews and surveys which included indigenous stakeholders and CBT operators and policymakers as research participants. The researchers used MAXQDA software to analyze data through thematic and axial coding methods which enabled them to discover main dimensions and their related occurrences. Findings The results show that GenAI can effectively address digital skill deficiencies while enabling indigenous practitioners to work independently. The study presents an updated Ability–Motivation–Opportunity (AMO) framework which introduces “Challenges” as a new element and shows how “Community Support” functions as a vital moderator of individual motivation. The research results demonstrate that GenAI can effectively close digital skill gaps while enhancing indigenous people’s skills through CBT and promoting their independence and social connections. The system becomes inaccessible to users because digital infrastructure limitations and public knowledge deficiencies combine with policy development shortcomings. Practical implications Successful integration requires policy interventions which need to address digital infrastructure and literacy and regulatory trust. GenAI-mediated CBT through its ability to create sustainable communities (Sustainable Development Goal [SDG] 11) and reduce poverty (SDG 1) helps preserve tribal values and their cultural heritage. The research shows that targeted skill development programs need to exist together with policy measures which will help communities achieve their optimal GenAI benefits for sustainable income generation and employment. Originality/value This research addresses a severe dearth of literature regarding GenAI integration into indigenous homestay operations. The study presents an original theoretical framework which demonstrates through empirical evidence how advanced AI technologies link to environmental sustainability objectives in rural areas. There is very limited published literature on GenAI technology integration into homestay operations amongst indigenous communities. The findings of this study present unique insights which have not been documented in previous research.

Raw data for study: Systematic literature reviews (SLRs) are highly valuable to researchers and practitioners because they provide rigorous, unbiased summaries of existing evidence, identify alternative approaches to problem solving, and reveal knowledge gaps that can guide future research. However, conducting an SLR can be laborious and time consuming, particularly during full-text screening and data extraction, and it is natural to ask whether Large Language Models (LLMs) can accelerate the process. LLMs may reduce reviewer workload, but it is still unclear how closely their judgments align with human reviewers, whether their outputs may influence human decisions, and how much human oversight is needed. This study evaluates the data extraction phase of the PRISMA (Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses) process. We report on the inter-rater reliability (using Krippendorff's $\alpha$) between human reviewers with and without LLM output (coding and evidential text), between consensus codes agreed before and after consulting LLM output, and with and without access to LLM output during data extraction. We conclude that there is strong evidence that access to LLM output accelerates human reviewers' convergence without noticeably biasing that consensus. We propose an approach to incorporate LLMs into the coding process, while maintaining the supervision of human researchers. Based on preliminary benchmarks, we expect at least a four-times speedup, mostly due to the use of the LLM coding and evidence by the human reviewer as a starting point for their coding.

Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used in software pipelines, raising concerns about harmful behaviors in security-critical domains. Existing safety evaluations predominantly probe models with single prompts or short interactions, and therefore do not capture how safety behaves under multi-step workflows where individual requests are composed into complex behavior. This paper introduces compositional safety, the property that an LLM remains safe not only against isolated malicious prompts, but also under structured, long-horizon decompositions of harmful intents. We propose CAST, a systematic testing framework designed to evaluate the compositional safety of LLMs in the domain of malicious code. Drawing inspiration from modern compiler infrastructures, CAST decouples test case generation from test execution using a novel intermediate representation, CAIR. This architecture allows the framework to automatically refine high-level testing intents into granular sub-tasks that serve as unit tests for the model’s alignment. These components are subsequently instantiated by the SUT and reassembled according to the CAIR control structure. The resulting artifact is then evaluated by intent-fulfillment scoring and, for the severity subset, external behavioral detectors and manual inspection. We evaluate CAST on four state-of-the-art LLMs across three security-critical testbeds. Our results demonstrate that CAST systematically exposes severe safety violations in strongly aligned models that resist conventional red-teaming, achieving up to a 365% increase in successful test cases compared to baseline testing strategies

Change is the only thing believed to be constant in this world, as everything takes a new form at one time or another. Artificial intelligence (AI) is the “new normal” that has rapidly changed our world. This article explores the emergence of Artificial Intelligence and its roles in Modern Society, the concept of Christian leadership and Church administration, the nexus between Artificial Intelligence and Christian leadership with Church Administration, and the challenges of integrating AI into Christian leadership and administration within a local Church assembly. It also proposes solutions for integrating Artificial Intelligence and Christian leadership with Church administration. This study reveals that although AI could be integrated into the administrative aspect of the Church to enhance the leadership’s effectiveness and efficiency in Church management, it should never replace human interaction and fellowship, which are germane in Church ministries.

Artificial intelligence (AI)-supported learning is increasingly used in medical education, including doctor–patient communication training. Such systems may provide virtual dialogue practice, immediate structured feedback, reflection prompts and opportunities for further practice after feedback. However, educational usefulness does not necessarily imply ethical acceptability. This study examined changes in medical students’ ethical and acceptability-related perceptions before and after participation in an AI-supported doctor–patient communication learning pathway. This longitudinal empirical ethics survey was nested within a course-based randomised educational trial but was analytically independent of the parent trial’s educational outcome analysis. Surveys were administered after random allocation to the AI-supported pathway but before exposure to AI-supported learning functions (T0), at the end of the 8-week course (T1), and at the 3-month follow-up (T2). The main analysis focused on students in the AI-supported pathway with complete T0–T1–T2 ethics-related scale data and analysable T2 open-text responses ( n = 31). The open-text question was included only at T2. The primary comparison was the within-participant T0–T2 change across six ethics-related domains. Two domains showed statistically significant T0–T2 changes. Trust in AI feedback decreased from 3.86 (0.55) to 3.20 (0.62), with a mean change of − 0.66 (95% confidence interval [CI] − 0.88 to − 0.42), Cohen’s d z = − 1.04 and Holm–Bonferroni-adjusted p < 0.001. Room to question AI outputs increased from 2.71 (0.68) to 3.67 (0.58), with a mean change of 0.96 (95% CI 0.69 to 1.23), Cohen’s d z = 1.29 and Holm–Bonferroni-adjusted p < 0.001. The remaining four domains showed small, non-significant changes after Holm–Bonferroni correction. T2 open-text responses indicated that students recognised the formative value of AI feedback while emphasising critical use, teacher supervision, preservation of interpersonal interaction and clearer data governance. This exploratory longitudinal empirical ethics survey showed that, following participation in an AI-supported doctor–patient communication learning pathway, two of the six ethics-related domains showed statistically significant changes: trust in AI feedback decreased, while perceived room to question AI outputs increased. These findings support continued attention to ethics-focused evaluation and clear governance arrangements in AI-supported learning pathways.

documents.abstract: The study examines the growing presence of generative artificial intelligence in education and focuses on teachers' perceptions of ChatGPT as a support tool in the teaching and learning process. The development of AI is transforming teaching practices by enabling content personalisation, the creation of educational materials, and more efficient lesson preparation; at the same time, it raises questions about the reliability of generated content, ethical considerations, and teachers' digital competencies. In the context of the specific characteristics of the Polish education system—an ageing workforce, the feminisation of the profession, and the outflow of young teachers—the implementation of technological innovations may be uneven. The study aims to explore teachers’ familiarity with ChatGPT, its use in their daily practice, and the barriers and concerns associated with its adoption. The findings contribute to the discussion on the responsible integration of AI in education and indicate directions for teachers’ professional development.

documents.abstract: The rapid evolution of Artificial Intelligence (AI) has a significant influence on various aspects of human life. While there are numerous benefits from utilising AI tools, excessive dependence on them in education raises concerns, especially with regard to youth mental health. This study examines the possible effects of overreliance on Artificial Intelligence (AI) tools on youth mental health. It explores the role of Christian educators in addressing these challenges. The paper provides an overview of mental health by emphasising its multifaceted nature and encompassing emotional, psychological, cognitive, and social well-being. The paper argues that although AI tools have revolutionised education and have led to improvements and productivity, their overuse among young people raises concerns about mental health implications. Such mental health implications include diminished critical thinking, reduced autonomy, impaired memory skills, and social isolation. Moreover, the paper highlights the role of Christian educators in addressing the excessive usage of Artificial Intelligence (AI) tools. The strategies proposed for combating the concern are AI literacy, curriculum development, mental health awareness, and promoting balanced learning approaches. As Christian educators integrate biblical principles and responsible AI use, the negative effect of AI overdependence among youth will be alleviated.

documents.abstract: ABSTRACT Job advertisements play a crucial role in attracting applicants, yet little is known about how closely they reflect the values citizens expect from public servants. Drawing on signaling theory and prior research on citizens' normative expectations of ideal public servants, this study employs a large language model to analyze 1825 job advertisements from health and transportation departments across seven U.S. states. Compared to the values citizens associate with ideal public servants in previous research, job advertisements predominantly emphasize values, such as expertise and dedication, while undersignaling relational values like serviceability, responsiveness, and honesty. Our findings suggest a misalignment between the values signaled in recruitment practices and those citizens associate with the ideal public servant. By adopting a citizen‐driven perspective, this study prompts scholars and public managers to question recruitment practices that may underemphasize values citizens prioritize in public servants, potentially limiting public administrations' ability to attract qualified candidates.

BACKGROUND: The classification of adventure activities and sports lacks a single consensus and has been addressed by a variety of studies and distinct perspectives. By focusing on the evolution of technological resources, particularly Artificial Intelligence chatbots, it is expected that this topic may receive a contemporary and multifaceted approach, which may contribute to a broader understanding of this theme in a global context. OBJECTIVE: This aspect motivated the present study, whose objective was to investigate the perspective produced by the Perplexity chatbot regarding the current classification of adventure activities and sports across the five continents. METHODS: This qualitative study was conducted by applying a similar prompt for each of the five continents, asking: “How is the classification of adventure activities and sports carried out in different countries of …?”. Data were analyzed using the Multimodal Content Analysis technique.RESULTS: The results revealed that categorization based on the explored environment is a common criterion. However, particularities emerged based on levels of risk, organizational regulations, and safety certifications, which vary regionally. Furthermore, the classifications generated did not incorporate practices in urban environments, indicating a significant gap.CONCLUSION: The study revealed that the classification of adventure activities and sports is multifaceted on an international level. It is evident that these classifications are predominantly organized based on environmental categories (land, water, ice/snow, and air), supplemented by criteria related to risk, accessibility, and the human and technological conditions of performance.

Abstract Accurate cytological evaluation of body fluid specimens is essential for diagnosing inflammatory and malignant conditions, yet manual interpretation remains labor-intensive and subject to inter-observer variability. This study developed and deployed a smartphone-based deep learning framework for multi-class body fluid cell classification integrating object detection, ROI-based classification, and explainable artificial intelligence (XAI). Three hundred Wright–Giemsa–stained cytospin slides, one per patient, were used to generate 7149 smartphone-acquired images, which were annotated and curated into seven predominant cell classes. To reduce data leakage, images were partitioned at the source-photograph (slide-field) level. Five detection architectures (YOLOv8n, YOLOv10n, YOLOv11n, YOLOv11n-seg, and RT-DETR) were trained and evaluated on a held-out test set. YOLOv11n-seg achieved the highest mAP@50 (0.840), mAP@50–95 (0.757), and precision (0.772), while YOLOv11n achieved the highest recall (0.823). For YOLOv11n-seg, confusion-matrix macro-F1 and weighted-F1 were 0.720 and 0.730, respectively. Eosinophils, lymphocytes, and neutrophils were among the better-recognized classes, whereas errors were more frequent among monocytes, macrophages, and mesothelial cells. Grad-CAM++ analysis showed that model activation was predominantly centered within cell regions but was interpreted only as supportive model-inspection evidence. A Streamlit web application demonstrated browser-based inference with detection overlays, cell counts, differential composition, and data export. The system should currently be regarded as research, educational, and decision-support prototype rather than a standalone diagnostic device. External validation with patient-level separation, multiple imaging configurations, and broader cell populations is required before clinical application can be considered.

As Code Large Language Models (LLMs) become central to modern software engineering, their inherent stochasticity poses significant real-world risks, where even minor errors can lead to severe functional, security, or safety consequences. Reliable automation, therefore, demands the ability to distinguish between confident, well-supported predictions and stochastic guessing. However, existing uncertainty estimation methods face a critical gap: white-box and grey-box techniques are often inapplicable to closed-source models, while standard black-box text metrics fail to capture the unique fragility of code, where syntactic variation does not necessarily imply semantic divergence. To bridge this syntax-semantics gap, we introduce Code-MUE, a purely black-box framework that measures uncertainty through execution-based Semantic Interaction Graphs. Unlike prior approaches that rely on superficial textual similarity, Code-MUE grounds uncertainty in observable runtime behavior and calculates the von Neumann entropy of the solution space to quantify global semantic diversity. A large-scale empirical study across eight state-of-the-art LLMs demonstrates that Code-MUE achieves a strong negative correlation with functional correctness, with Spearman’s correlation reaching up to −0.98. It significantly outperforms lexical and embedding-based baselines while enabling robust risk detection and selective prediction in practical workflows.

User Stories are key artifacts in Requirement and Software Engineering. Despite their wide adoption, their writing in industrial contexts tends to diverge from the principles initially stated in Agile methodologies. In this context, sets of metrics such as INVEST or QUS emerged to qualify these items. In this paper, we argue that the said sets of metrics are only partially efficient at capturing the quality of user stories contextualized in a project, and that their actual adoption in business contexts is limited due to multiple aspects: their unfitness to specific contexts, the difficulty of implementation requiring human intervention, the absence of reproducibility or their misalignment with actual quality of user stories. Such limitations, prevent practitioners from efficiently applying them for downstream tasks such as LLM-based user story generation. To address these challenges, we introduce COEUR, a framework comprising two metrics: Cohesion and Exhaustiveness. These metrics are designed to mirror core Product Owner responsibilities. Specifically, Cohesion evaluates the structural organization and logical grouping of the backlog, while Exhaustiveness monitors the semantic alignment between the elicited needs and the proposed technical solutions. Additionally, they are quantitative, reproducible, and automatically computable. To evaluate COEUR, we conduct four empirical experiments organized into two validation tracks. The first track utilizes two noising-based experiments to assess our metrics' sensitivity to requirement degradation. The second track evaluates their performance in generative contexts through two standard learning paradigms for LLMs: In-Context Learning (ICL) and Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT), both applied to our user story generation task. Subsequently, COEUR provides a turnkey measurement of Product Backlogs' quality for both project monitoring by human experts and LLM benchmarking applied to automatic user stories generation.

David Brooks's cautionary framework on cognitive polarization—wherein individuals with high need-for-cognition leverage AI to amplify capacity while others outsource thinking entirely—presents organizations with an urgent strategic imperative. This article synthesizes research on workplace AI adoption, employee development, and organizational psychology to examine how enterprises can prevent the emergence of a "mental underclass" while capturing AI's productivity benefits. Evidence demonstrates that cognitive engagement patterns are shaped less by innate traits than by organizational design, learning culture, and job architecture. Organizations that frame AI as an augmentation partner rather than a substitution tool, embed reflective practice into workflows, democratize access to cognitively enriching tasks, and cultivate psychological safety around experimentation show measurably higher workforce capability development alongside productivity gains. Through examination of interventions spanning interface design, learning infrastructure, work redesign, and leadership communication across manufacturing, professional services, healthcare, and financial sectors, this article provides actionable guidance for HR leaders, learning officers, and executives navigating the dual mandate of technological adoption and human capital development. The conclusion emphasizes that organizational choices—not individual cognitive disposition—will largely determine whether AI widens or narrows capability gaps within the workforce.

documents.abstract: Cooperative Perception (CP) supports autonomous driving by enabling connected autonomous vehicles (CAVs) to share sensor data, thereby increasing situational awareness and safety. However, training CP models requires diverse traffic scenarios, and real-world datasets are limited due to the high cost of multi-agent setups and the labor-intensive nature of labeling. Synthetic datasets offer a scalable alternative, but models trained exclusively on virtual data often face domain adaptation challenges. This paper presents a systematic benchmark that evaluates two advanced 3D LiDAR-based object detectors on synthetic and real datasets using three strategies: training from scratch, transferring from synthetic to real data, and training with mixed datasets. The results show that pre-training on synthetic data followed by fine-tuning on real datasets yields the best performance (+2% AP@0.5, +2-4% AP@0.7 for car detection), while mixed training improves cross-domain generalization. These findings underscore the value of synthetic data as a complementary resource for developing robust CP systems.

Precise measurement of color discrimination across color space is limited by the time and effort required to collect large psychophysical datasets. We investigated whether immersive virtual reality (VR) can support high-throughput measurement of color discrimination without compromising data quality. A standard four-alternative forced-choice odd-one-out task was embedded in an interactive VR environment inspired by the rhythm game Beat Saber, in which participants indicated the location of a chromatic target by slicing approaching cubes. Stimuli were presented on a color-calibrated VR headset, and chromaticities were specified in DKL space. Discrimination thresholds were measured for hue and chroma shifts around two reference colors. Participants sustained response rates of approximately one trial per second while maintaining stable performance. Thresholds replicated established asymmetries in color discrimination: hue thresholds were lower than chroma thresholds, and the hue-chroma ratio differed between color quadrants. A control experiment comparing VR-based slicing responses with matched keyboard responses revealed comparable psychometric fits and threshold estimates, indicating that motor engagement did not degrade measurement precision. Questionnaire measures further showed significantly higher intrinsic motivation, enjoyment, and stimulation in the immersive condition relative to a classic static psychophysical task, without increases in reported pressure or discomfort. These results demonstrate that calibrated immersive VR can yield reliable color discrimination measurements at substantially increased throughput, providing a scalable approach for mapping the metric structure of color space.

It’s that time of year again in Houston. From 21 to 23 October, SPE will host thousands of oil and gas industry professionals at its 102nd Annual Technical Conference and Exhibition (ATCE) at the George R. Brown Convention Center. The theme of this year’s gathering is Exploring New Horizons with Innovative Solutions, which also serves as a call to action. Over the past decade, the industry has undergone tremendous change, and technology has often been central to how it has adapted. Over that span, we experienced the 2014 to 2016 oil price crash, which upended countless companies and led to massive layoffs across the industry. In January 2014, Brent crude traded above $107/bbl. A year later, it had fallen to little more than $50/bbl. The slide continued, and by January 2016 prices had dropped to roughly $32.50/bbl. The 2-year downturn that ushered in the era of “lower for longer” was driven in large part by the technological advances that enabled the rise of the North American shale revolution. Markets ultimately recognized that tight oil had materially altered the global supply picture. Just as the industry regained its footing, prices swung sharply again in 2018. Brent climbed to a 4-year high of about $86/bbl in October before falling to $50/bbl by December. During this downturn, particularly among US tight-oil and -gas producers, capital discipline became the defining business strategy as companies faced renewed pressure to improve returns while controlling spending. The pain was real. US oil and gas companies with significant shale exposure collectively lost nearly 30% of their value, while oilfield service providers saw approximately 40% erased from their market capitalization during the downturn. Few in the industry need to be reminded of the disruption that accompanied the onset of the COVID-19 pandemic that swept the industry off its feet just 1 year later. Economies around the world slowed dramatically. Highways emptied, airports went silent, and supply chains were broken. For those of us in the upstream sector, the market shock produced another seemingly unimaginable event. As Brent crude fell to about $14/bbl in April 2020, the US benchmark West Texas Intermediate (WTI) briefly traded at negative prices, reaching –$37.63/bbl as storage constraints and market dislocation forced overextended traders to offload positions at almost any cost. But 2 years later, economies reopened and the pandemic receded. Negative oil prices became something of a historical anomaly. Then Russia’s invasion of Ukraine in early 2022 sent energy markets into another period of turmoil, driving Brent crude above $125/bbl. That was 4 years ago. And prices retreated again as the world speculated that we were facing yet another oil glut. At the start of this year, many expected oil prices to settle into a range near $60/bbl. Instead, ongoing geopolitical tensions have once again defied market expectations. With the conflict between the US and Iran stretching out for more than 6 months, both Brent and WTI climbed above $100/bbl in September amid supply disruptions and growing concerns over global inventories. This brief walk down memory lane brings us back to ATCE’s theme this year of new horizons and innovative solutions. Over the past decade, the industry has repeatedly been forced to do more with less. The upside of these painful episodes is that producers today are more efficient than ever before and are generating record levels of production with fewer resources than many would have considered possible only a decade ago. But even as we look at $100/bbl oil prices today, few are cheering for them to go higher. The industry understands there is a breaking point for consumers and that demand destruction tends to have significant and lasting consequences. At ATCE, attendees will hear how some of the world’s leading energy producers are dealing with all this uncertainty, which many consider to be a hallmark of our new normal. Discussions will also address the industry’s effort to decarbonize while still helping billions of people get to work, keep their lights on, and heat their homes. Attendees will also learn more about the industry’s digital transformation, which has now been supercharged by the advent of advanced artificial intelligence (AI) programs, often referred to as frontier models. The rise of AI has been anticipated for years, but the widespread excitement, controversy, and debate surrounding its capabilities suggest that we are truly entering a new era of computing and software. Where AI ultimately leads us all remains difficult to predict. What is clear is that the industry’s mission remains unchanged. The business must continue to operate safely, remain resilient in the face of market uncertainty, and responsibly deliver the energy needed to fuel economic progress. New technologies, particularly AI, will play a major role in this effort if they are able to enhance human expertise and help organizations make better decisions. Several industry leaders will share their perspectives on these topics during ATCE’s Opening General Session. Moderated by 2026 SPE President Jennifer Miskimins, the panel will feature Ahmed Alebri, CEO of ADNOC Onshore; Peter Larden, senior vice president of upstream, conventional, and heavy oil for ExxonMobil; Lorenzo Simonelli, chairman and CEO of Baker Hughes; and Ezra Yacob, chairman and CEO of EOG Resources. Additional panels and technical sessions will explore topics including agentic AI, growing energy demand from data centers, and the challenge of improving recovery from unconventional reservoirs as many of the most productive US shale plays continue to mature. One more thing that attendees can expect to find in the SPE Pavilion this year is a special print edition of JPT, produced in partnership with the not-for-profit organization Project InnerSpace. The special issue features original JPT articles and technical paper synopses focused on next-generation geothermal systems. Our goal is to help oil and gas professionals better understand how the industry’s expertise, technologies, and decades of subsurface experience can contribute to the progress being made in this growing field of subsurface engineering. It is an exciting time for the oil and gas industry, but it is not free of major challenges. At ATCE, many of those challenges will be discussed and debated by the engineers, scientists, executives, and technical professionals working to identify practical solutions. I hope many of you will be part of those conversations and help shape the future of our industry when you return to your organizations. As I often do, I would also like to thank the many SPE members and volunteers who have devoted countless hours to organizing ATCE and the SPE’s other events throughout the year. Their efforts help make SPE the industry’s unrivaled forum for advancing petroleum engineering knowledge and sharing technical expertise. Much of that work takes place behind the scenes, but it is deeply appreciated by all of us at JPT. For more information about ATCE 2026 and to register, please visit the conference website.

The hierarchy of controls framework prioritizes engineering solutions over administrative measures and personal protective equipment, yet oil drilling operations typically invert this approach. This mixed-methods comparative effectiveness study evaluated 400 workers across 15 drilling sites implementing different control strategies over 18 months. Engineering-dominant sites demonstrated 61% lower chronic respiratory disease incidence (HR=0.39, 95% CI: 0.23- 0.66) and 56% lower musculoskeletal disorders (HR=0.44, 95% CI: 0.28-0.69) compared to PPEreliant sites. Cost-effectiveness analysis revealed engineering controls achieved ₦19,840,000 ($12,400) per Quality-Adjusted Life Year (QALY) gained versus ₦82,880,000 ($51,800) for administrative controls and ₦109,120,000 ($68,200) for PPE programmes. However, engineering control effectiveness degraded 47% over 18 months without adequate maintenance, while administrative compliance declined from 78% to 34%. Qualitative analysis identified six implementation barriers: capital investment resistance (87% of sites), production-safety conflicts (73%), maintenance system inadequacy (93%), management turnover disrupting continuity (67%), worker skepticism from past failures (73%), and chronic disease invisibility preventing urgency (93%). Findings demonstrate engineering controls' superior effectiveness and cost-efficiency while revealing that implementation sustainability determines real-world impact. Meaningful chronic disease prevention requires regulatory mandates prioritizing engineering solutions, adequate maintenance systems, organizational accountability for health outcomes, and long-term monitoring capturing delayed disease manifestations

The analysis of histopathological images is an important method of diagnosing cancer. Deep learning models, such as convolutional neural networks and transformer-based models have demonstrated great potential in automated cancer detection. However, they are black-box and cannot be understood in a clinical context. In this paper, a comparative study is conducted to analyze the explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) approaches for cancer detection based on histopathology images on a hybrid model based on deep learning networks: ResNet-18 and Vision Transformer (ViT). The hybrid model is trained on histopathology images and three explainability mechanisms are used, including Grad-CAM, Grad-CAM++, and Score-CAM to visualize regions of decisions made. The created heatmaps are evaluated according to the accuracy of localization, noise minimization, and interpretability. Experimental results indicate that Grad-CAM++ provides better localization and Score-CAM generates more smooth and noisy explanations. This comparative analysis enhances transparency of models and helps to make more credible medical decisions.

Large Language Models (LLMs) have significantly improved programming efficiency by parsing natural language into code snippets. However, their performance degrades significantly as requirements scale; when faced with multi-modal documents containing hundreds of scenarios, LLMs often produce incorrect implementations or omit crucial constraints. Observing LLMs' ever-evolving capability and their persistent stochastic hallucination, we raise a question: whether it is possible to make LLM-based agentic programming go beyond "code generation" to "requirement compilation", i.e., whether programmers can produce a runnable system by only accomplishing (non-trivial) requirement documents? In this work, we take a first step by proposing the ARC (Agentic Requirement Compilation) technique to parse a multi-modal requirement document, describing hundreds of scenarios in a DSL format, into a runnable software system. In addition to the source code, ARC also generates software engineering artifacts including (1) a modular design that spans the user interface, API interface, and database, (2) enriched test cases for each interface (including unit tests, modular tests, and integration tests), and (3) detailed traceability across all artifacts for software maintenance. Our approach employs a bidirectional test-driven agentic loop: (1) a top-down architecture phase that decomposes requirements into UI, API, and database interfaces, each of which is equipped with verifiable test suites, and (2) a bottom-up implementation phase where agents generate code that must satisfy the generated tests. Throughout this process, ARC maintains strict traceability across requirements, design, and code to facilitate intelligent asset reuse and follow-up maintenance. We evaluate ARC on two complementary benchmarks, i.e., a depth-oriented benchmark of 6 runnable web systems spanning 50-200 requirement scenarios, and the breadth-oriented AppForge benchmark comprising 101 Android app generation tasks. Across 3 independent trials, ARC outperforms all state-of-the-art LLM-based baselines, with the generated web systems passing on average 50.6% more GUI tests, and achieving 100% compile success and 68.3% test case pass rate on AppForge. In addition, a user study with 21 participants shows that participants with limited programming experience successfully write DSL-based documents consisting of 50 to 174 scenarios, within 5.6 hours on average, to generate a runnable system such as a real-world ticket-booking system of around 10K lines of code with maintainable architecture.

RAISINS (R and AI Solutions for INferential Statistics) is an advanced, user-friendly online platform for statistical analysis, seamlessly integrating the power of R, Python, and Artificial Intelligence. Specially designed for agricultural research, RAISINS enables students, researchers, and professionals to perform complex analyses and generate publication-ready results without the need for software installation or coding expertise. Simply choose your analysis module, upload your dataset, and receive instant, insightful outputs. RAISINS supports individual users across the globe as well as institutions in India and abroad. This Computational Provenance and Reproducibility Record documents the statistical computing environment, software dependencies, computational provenance, and bibliographic references associated with the RAISINS Pooled 2FCRD module. It is intended to support computational reproducibility and software transparency. Detailed statistical methodology, mathematical derivations, and user guidance are provided separately in the official module documentation. You can access the online cloud platform at https://www.raisins.live/

Rising student absenteeism remains a persistent challenge in higher education, potentially exacerbated by the growing use of artificial intelligence (AI) tools. Drawing on digital displacement theory, this study examines whether general AI use is associated with students’ self-efficacy for independent learning and absenteeism. Survey data from 291 Portuguese university students were analysed using partial least squares structural equation modelling, explaining 38.7% of the variance in absenteeism and 34.4% in self-efficacy. Internal locus of control, peer influence, time management, and AI use emerged as significant predictors. General AI use was positively associated with both self-efficacy and absenteeism, suggesting that AI may strengthen independent learning confidence while coinciding with reduced face-to-face engagement. Multigroup analysis provided exploratory evidence of gender differences, with the AI use–self-efficacy relationship stronger among males at the 5% level, while other gender differences appeared only at a more lenient 10% threshold.

Connecting Young Minds (CYM) is the University of Ottawa’s largest bilingual undergraduate Science, Technology, Engineering, and Mathematics (STEM) research conference dedicated to advancing student-led scientific innovation, interdisciplinary collaboration, and research communication. Organized by students, CYM provides undergraduate researchers with a platform to present original research and proposals through 5-minute scientific presentations followed by question-and-answer periods evaluated by expert judges. In 2025, the conference introduced poster presentations, enabling students to further engage with judges, keynote speakers, researchers, and attendees through interactive scientific discussion. The conference featured diverse projects spanning health sciences, engineering, natural sciences, artificial intelligence, environmental sciences, and biotechnology, reflecting the interdisciplinary nature of modern STEM research. Beyond the conference, CYM organized multiple fundraising initiatives supporting undergraduate scientific research, raising over CA$50,000, while its scientific outreach initiatives generated more than 2,000,000 social media views. Across all CYM events in 2025, over 800 attendees participated, including more than 300 attendees at this fully booked conference. As the University of Ottawa’s leading bilingual undergraduate STEM research conference, CYM continues to foster scientific engagement and innovation among emerging researchers. Abstracts in this booklet were submitted by participants on a volunteer basis.

documents.abstract: Abstract This paper critically examines the emerging sociotechnical visions of biochar within UK agriculture, focusing on its potential role in greenhouse gas removal (GGR) and the broader net zero agenda. Agriculture is framed as both a significant source of greenhouse gas emissions and a unique sector capable of acting as a carbon sink, positioning it at the heart of debates about climate change mitigation. The paper adopts a sociotechnical visions framework to illuminate how stakeholders align with, contest, and propose alternatives to the dominant net zero sociotechnical imaginary. We identify two overarching sociotechnical visions of biochar in UK agriculture. The first is a sociotechnical vision of greenhouse gas removal through biochar produced at scale and applied to agricultural land, detailing both farmer alignment with and contestation of this approach. The second is a sociotechnical vision of biochar for multiple on-farm benefits, including farm business benefits, enhanced agricultural production and improved on-farm biodiversity. The analysis shows that the future of biochar in UK agriculture is characterised by diversity and contestation, requiring governance frameworks that accommodate multiple, sometimes competing, sociotechnical visions. This pluralism offers opportunities for more just, inclusive, achievable, and transformative pathways for biochar in UK agriculture. Additionally, the paper contributes to the literature on sociotechnical imaginaries and sociotechnical visions by foregrounding the dynamic interplay and negotiation between top-down institutional imaginaries—such as net zero—and emergent, grassroots visions developed by farmers and other agricultural stakeholders.

documents.abstract: Text-to-SQL models translate natural language questions into SQL, enabling non-technical users to access databases. However, most existing research focuses on correctness, neglecting query efficiency. In this paper, we address the challenge of evaluating the execution efficiency of generated SQL in Text-to-SQL by introducing EESQLBench, a novel benchmark designed to assess both correctness and efficiency. EESQLBench pairs each natural language question with an expert-optimized SQL query, providing a reliable efficiency baseline. We evaluate six representative large language models (LLMs), including four open-source models (SQLCoder, CodeLlama, DeepSeek-Coder, and DeepSeek-R1) and two closed-source models (GPT-5.2 and Gemini-2.5-Pro), using cost-based metrics including Cost Reachability (CR) and Acceptable Reachability at kk (AR@kk). Our results reveal that current LLMs, despite achieving high correctness, struggle to produce efficient queries. We observe substantial efficiency gaps between models and emphasize that semantic correctness alone does not guarantee query efficiency. Furthermore, we provide insights into common inefficiency patterns in LLM-generated SQL queries, such as missing access pruning and inefficient subquery logic.

documents.abstract: This chapter offers an in-depth discussion of the possibilities of incorporating creativity, design thinking, and innovation into STEAM education with the help of the strategic implementation of artificial intelligence (AI) and digital technologies. At a time when the economy of knowledge requires flexible, problem solvers, STEAM models provide an interdisciplinary approach to the development of such skills. Nonetheless, conventional methods are usually not effective in developing actual creative thinking. The generative models and intelligent tutoring systems, bridges this gap by providing individualized, iterative, and immersive learning experiences. Based on educational psychology, instructional design, and developing AI pedagogies, the chapter defines major constructs, studies the role of technology, introduces practical models and deals with ethical issues. It adds to the overall discussion in Advancing STEAM Education at the Intersection of AI and Digital Technologies that highlights human centered innovation as a key component instead of technological determinism.

Background/Objectives: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly used to support chest radiograph interpretation, but its clinical value depends not only on stand-alone accuracy but also on whether its errors differ from those of clinicians. We evaluated CT-referenced, target-specific diagnostic performance and complementary error patterns of a commercial chest radiograph AI system and a single emergency physician. Methods: In this retrospective, single-center, paired diagnostic accuracy study, 920 consecutive adults who underwent posteroanterior chest radiography and thoracic computed tomography (CT) within 4 h during the same emergency department encounter were included. A commercial AI system (hChestXR version 1) and a single blinded emergency physician independently assessed eight prespecified thoracic findings using CT as the reference standard. Paired differences were estimated with 10,000 patient-level bootstrap resamples and tested with exact McNemar tests with Holm adjustment. Exact-target complementarity and simulated same-target OR/AND rules were secondary exploratory analyses. Results: Across 7360 patient–target assessments, including 1232 CT-positive findings, AI had significantly greater Holm-adjusted sensitivity for pneumothorax (90.8% vs. 50.8%), nodule/mass (63.3% vs. 32.7%), and rib fracture (77.2% vs. 46.5%). AI-only detections were most frequent for pneumothorax (47.7%), nodule/mass (44.9%), and rib fracture (43.6%), whereas physician-only detections were most frequent for atelectasis (24.8%), pulmonary edema (21.0%), and lung opacity (19.7%). In exploratory pooled analyses, sensitivity was 73.0% for AI and 62.0% for the physician. Exploratory simulated same-target OR/AND analyses demonstrated a sensitivity–specificity trade-off across pooled patient–target assessments but did not represent observed AI-assisted clinical performance. Conclusions: The AI system and the single emergency-physician reader in the study showed target-dependent, partly non-overlapping error patterns in this CT-selected emergency cohort. The findings support prospective multireader evaluation of AI as a second-reader tool but do not establish benefit from real-time AI-assisted interpretation.

documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) in surgery and anesthesiology encompasses different tasks: risk prediction, hypotension alerts, video analysis, technical-skill assessment, surgical-duration estimation, and postoperative support. Treating them as one promise of “AI surgery” obscures essential distinctions among retrospective performance, external validation, prospective clinical utility, impact on processes or outcomes, and routine implementation. This whitepaper synthesizes selected applications rather than exhaustively cataloguing all subspecialties, robotic platforms, or simulation techniques. The evidence closest to clinical evaluation in anesthesiology is concentrated in intraoperative hypotension prediction. A systematic review and meta-analysis included eight randomized-trial reports; its published total of 568 participants includes overlap between a study and its substudy and does not represent unique individuals. Seven reports evaluated the Hypotension Prediction Index and one evaluated fuzzy-logic control. The hypotension meta-analysis including the largest trial did not find a statistically significant difference and showed high heterogeneity. Favorable results from small trials do not establish universal benefit: this is a narrow family of systems, populations, and protocols. In surgery, phase recognition and technical-skill assessment have systematic reviews, whereas models for complications, delirium, length of stay, and surgical duration remain dominated by retrospective development or limited validation. Latin America has direct evidence that should not be replaced by silent extrapolation. A Bogotá study evaluated models for surgical-duration estimation; Brazilian studies developed models for postoperative delirium and length of stay after coronary artery bypass grafting; and LASOS described perioperative outcomes across 17 countries. These sources demonstrate regional research and data capacity and a measurable perioperative burden; they do not demonstrate general clinical effectiveness of AI, routine implementation, or transportability across countries. The directed search identified few regional AI records compared with the international literature; statements about infrastructure, interoperability, and governance therefore also rely on regional sources and are labelled as implementation context or inference, not model performance. Central finding: AI can currently support bounded perioperative surveillance, prediction, analysis, training, and operational tasks. It cannot yet responsibly promise independent intraoperative decisions, replacement of surgical or anesthetic

The co-creation activities are therefore crucial to the development of the DST as they provide useful feedback necessary for the development of a beneficial and relevant DST. The report presents the PrAEctiCe DST Architecture designs that follows the JDL/DFIG (Joint Directors of Laboratories/Data Fusion Group) reference model for structured Artificial Intelligence (AI) showing the levels from level 0 to level 5 in details as specified in the Grant Agreement (GA). These designs were presented to the stakeholders during the co-creation workshops to enable them identify functionalities that were missing or those that were not important for them in discharging their mandates.

documents.abstract: Abstract The Internet of Things (IoT) is a revolutionary innovation that enables greater automation, efficiency, and ease of use across various domains. Cloud computing is an efficient solution for processing and analyzing the large volume of data generated by IoT components. Data flows from edge devices to cloud environments demand strong end-user authentication, advanced security, strong recovery procedures, and user privacy guarantees. This study presents a comprehensive survey of existing literature on security in cloud-based IoT environments. In addition, associated problems are identified, and practical solutions are suggested. Based on the literature review, shortcomings in current methods of addressing data protection and privacy threats are identified. Ensuring secure data transmission requires significant advances in cloud and IoT device architecture and the development of reliable communication protocols. Emerging technologies, including blockchain, artificial intelligence, fog computing, and edge computing, hold promising prospects. These technologies could mitigate the threats associated with centralized cloud storage. In this context, the leading security threats, categorizations, and reactive plans for protecting data in cloud-based IoT systems are comprehensively reviewed. Blockchain-assisted IoT authentication frameworks have been reported in prior studies to reduce authentication and verification latency by approximately 26–35% compared to centralized authentication schemes and Practical Byzantine Fault Tolerance (PBFT)-based baselines, as observed in simulation-based evaluations under controlled network conditions and specific system configurations. In parallel, machine learning-based intrusion detection systems, particularly deep learning and ensemble models, evaluated on benchmark datasets such as CICIDS2017, TON_IoT, and UNSW-NB15, have achieved classification accuracies exceeding 99% under certain experimental settings, depending on feature selection, model architecture, and dataset-balance constraints.

LLM agents that invoke external tools face critical safety vulnerabilities when malicious manipulations exploit their implicit trust in tool outputs and metadata. However, identifying these vulnerabilities through testing is challenging due to the need to bypass safety guardrails with semantically legitimate inputs, the difficulty in characterizing successful attacks amid implicit tool trust, and the requirement to maintain logical consistency across fragile state-dependent execution chains. In this paper, we first conduct an empirical study to investigate how external tools influence agent reasoning. Guided by the findings, we propose Datura, an automated red teaming testing framework that exposes safety vulnerabilities through chained tool manipulation. Through a five-stage workflow, Datura dynamically generates test cases where each individual step appears legitimate yet collectively leads to harmful outcomes. We evaluate Datura across five LLMs and 740 safety-critical tasks under five defense settings, including real-world safety mechanisms. Under Model Alignment, Datura achieves 94.86--99.59% attack success rate (ASR), outperforming the strongest baseline by up to 25.27 percentage points. Under Prompt Refuge, Datura maintains 78.78--95.54% ASR, showing that progressive tool-chain manipulation remains effective even under prompt-level safeguards.

While safety alignment and guardrails help large language models (LLMs) avoid harmful outputs, they can also induce overrefusal, i.e., unwarranted rejection of benign queries that merely appear risky. We present DDOR (Delta Debugging for OverRefusal), a fully automated and explainable framework for overrefusal testing and repair in a black-box setting, where only model inputs and outputs are accessible and internal safety mechanisms remain opaque. DDOR applies delta debugging to localize minimal refusal-triggering fragments (mRTFs) that provide phrase-level, explainable evidence for why a refusal occurs. Conditioned on these mRTFs, DDOR generates diverse, context-rich prompts and performs multi-oracle validation to filter intrinsically unsafe or ambiguous cases, producing scalable and model-specific overrefusal test suites (approximately 1K cases per model). Beyond evaluation, we further leverage localized mRTFs to perform targeted prompt repair, substantially reducing overrefusal while preserving the original intent and maintaining safety on genuinely harmful inputs. Overall, DDOR offers a practical end-to-end solution to both evaluate and mitigate overrefusal, improving LLM usability without sacrificing safety.

Health time series (HTS) provide a fundamental representation of dynamic health processes, spanning organ-level physiological signals, patient-level clinical trajectories, and population-level epidemic dynamics. Despite their shared temporal nature, existing surveys often study these categories separately, leaving their methodological connections underdeveloped. In this survey, we provide a unified review of deep learning for HTS, organized around a scarcity-driven methodological development trajectory. Specifically, we examine how label scarcity motivates task-specific supervised learning with domain-aware temporal modeling; how sample scarcity motivates foundation model development and generative augmentation; and how information scarcity motivates multi-modal learning by incorporating complementary clinical information. Finally, we summarize representative healthcare applications and open research directions. By connecting data categories, scarcity challenges, and methodological paradigms, this survey provides a structured roadmap for understanding and developing deep learning methods for HTS.

Abstract Convolutional neural networks (CNNs) are among the deep learning architectures driving the current artificial intelligence revolution and were initially developed for image processing. Image tensors can also be generated from timefrequency analyses such as the continuous wavelet transform (CWT). We investigate whether the combination of CWT and CNN can be successfully applied to the processing of short EEG segments during microsleep (MS) events. Our dataset consists of 24,156 MS and 18,686 counterexamples from five studies conducted in our driving simulator over the past 20 years. When comparing several CNN methods, the ResNet152 network proves to be most successful with accuracies of 96.8 ± 0.9 % after 10-fold cross-validation. This is comparable to the performance of standard machine learning using support vector machines (SVM), which yielded 96.3 ± 0.0 %.

With the rapid advancement of artificial intelligence, deep learning-based multimodal data fusion technology has found increasing applications in the field of dental and stomatological diseases, and it has demonstrated great potential. This technology constructs deep neural networks to automatically extract and fuse features from multimodal data, such as clinical text information, medical imaging, intraoral and extraoral digital scanning records, and histopathological data. By fully leveraging the complementary information among these diverse data sources, it substantially enhances the accuracy of oral disease diagnosis, the rationality of treatment planning, and the reliability of prognosis prediction. This survey systematically explores the core advantages of deep learning in multimodal data fusion; outlines key main strategies, such as early fusion, intermediate fusion, and late fusion along with their applicable scenarios; and summarizes the specific applications and latest research progress of this technology in oral diseases, including oral cancer, periodontitis, dental caries, and temporomandibular disorders. We also highlight critical challenges in its clinical translation, such as complexity in multimodal data alignment, scarcity of high-quality annotated data, insufficient model interpretability, and privacy and security issues. In the future, this technology is expected to develop toward new learning paradigms, intelligentization, and adaptive fusion while integrating explainable artificial intelligence to enhance clinical credibility. Ultimately, large-scale, multicenter clinical validation systems will be required to ensure its safe and effective deployment in clinical practice.

Survival analysis is fundamental to biomedical research and clinical decision-making, where outcomes such as mortality, disease progression, relapse, and time-to-discharge are frequently observed under censoring and competing risks. Recent advances in deep learning have expanded the capabilities of survival modeling by enabling flexible nonlinear representations of heterogeneous biomedical data, including electronic health records, medical imaging, and multi-omics profiles. This structured narrative review synthesizes studies published between 2018 and 2026, examining major deep survival model families, including neural extensions of the Cox proportional hazards model, discrete-time and distribution-based approaches, multimodal architectures, transformers, and emerging foundation-model paradigms. We critically compare deep learning approaches with classical and machine learning survival methods, highlighting the conditions under which increased model complexity provides meaningful advantages. We further examine representative biomedical applications, datasets, evaluation and benchmarking practices, with particular emphasis on calibration, competing risks, external validation, and model selection. The review identifies persistent challenges in generalization, sample size and event scarcity, censoring mechanisms, interpretability, fairness, reproducibility, and clinical translation, while outlining emerging directions toward robust, trustworthy, and clinically actionable survival modeling systems.

documents.abstract: We present , an Artificial Intelligence (AI) multiagent system designed to serve as a scientific research assistant. can perform many different tasks, such as generating ideas, checking the literature, developing research plans, writing and executing code, making plots, and drafting a scientific paper. The system has a modular architecture, allowing it to handle specific tasks, such as generating an idea or carrying out near end-to-end scientific analysis using as a deep-research backend (end-to-end except for the novelty assessment, which is intentionally left for the user to inspect). In this work, we describe in detail and its modules, and illustrate its capabilities by presenting multiple AI-generated papers generated by it in many different scientific disciplines such as astrophysics, biology, biophysics, biomedical informatics, chemistry, material science, mathematical physics, medicine, neuroscience, and planetary science. can also produce work that combines ideas from different disciplines, which we illustrate with a single ( N = 1 ) example: a paper that applies methods from quantum physics and machine learning to astrophysical data. We report the evaluations performed on these papers by domain experts, who provided both numerical scores and reviewlike feedback. These papers were scored by domain experts on our team; we report these scores as an indicative self-assessment rather than an independent evaluation, and we flag the resulting conflict of interest explicitly. Most drafts were rated above the midpoint of a 0–10 scale, with several rated 8–9, indicating that the generated papers reach the level a good undergraduate or early graduate student could achieve after weeks or a few months of work. They should be regarded as first drafts that require expert development, not publication-ready papers. We also document an important failure mode in which, when the input data cannot be read, the system may silently generate synthetic data, which we flag explicitly as a key limitation. We then highlight the strengths, weaknesses, and limitations of the current system. Finally, we discuss the ethical implications of AI-driven research and reflect on how such technology relates to the philosophy of science. We publicly release the code at . A demo can also be run directly on the web at , and the full app will be deployed on the cloud.

documents.abstract: Industrial Control Systems (ICS) in critical infrastructure remain highly exposed to cyber threats while operating under technical, operational, and regulatory constraints that often limit direct modification, update, or replacement. Existing surveys either provide broad overviews of ICS security or focus narrowly on Artificial Intelligence (AI)/Machine Learning (ML) methods, but rarely translate the evidence into deployment-oriented guidance for protecting legacy systems in brownfield environments. This paper presents a systematic review of 84 peer-reviewed studies published between 2021 and 2026, examining how AI/ML-based anomaly detection and compensating security controls can be combined within defence-in-depth architectures for legacy ICS. The review organises detection approaches by deployment zone within the Purdue architecture and learning paradigm, and relates major categories of compensating controls, such as network segmentation, unidirectional gateways, virtual patching, and Operational Technology (OT)-adapted Zero Trust architectures, to the IEC 62443 Security Levels. The evidence shows that no single detection architecture dominates across deployment scenarios, that benchmark performance alone does not establish operational readiness, and that AI/ML detection works best as a layer augmenting foundational controls rather than replacing them. It also identifies persistent weaknesses in cross-dataset validation and the continuing gap between reported model performance and real-world deployability. This review translates the literature into deployment-oriented guidance for asset owners, plant operators, and OT security architects, showing how detection and compensating controls can be combined across Purdue zones and IEC 62443 Security Levels to improve visibility, containment, and resilience without compromising operational continuity in legacy industrial environments.

Abstract Background: Accurate assessment of alveolar ridge width is essential for implant treatment planning. Although cone-beam computed tomography provides detailed three-dimensional information, chairside ridge-mapping techniques remain valuable because of their simplicity, accessibility, and cost-effectiveness. Objective: The objective of this study was to describe the design, clinical application, and potential advantages of a novel dental bone mapping caliper for transgingival ridge assessment. Technical Description: The proposed instrument incorporates a blunt external reference arm, a controlled transgingival probing tip, a calibrated sliding measurement scale, and an ergonomically designed handle within a single device. The instrument enables direct chairside measurement of alveolar ridge width while improving stabilization and measurement standardization. Clinical Application: The caliper is used during transgingival ridge mapping by positioning the blunt arm against the mucosal surface and advancing the probing tip until cortical bone contact is achieved. Measurements are recorded directly from the calibrated scale. Discussion: Compared with conventional ridge-mapping methods, the proposed design offers improved operator control, direct measurement recording, enhanced stability, and simplified clinical workflow. However, clinical validation studies are required to determine its accuracy, reproducibility, and patient acceptance. Conclusion: The novel dental bone mapping caliper represents a practical chairside tool for ridge assessment and may improve the standardization of transgingival bone mapping procedures. Further clinical investigations are necessary to establish its effectiveness relative to existing methods.

Conversational artificial intelligence (AI) assistants are proliferating, yet direct-answer interaction can yield short-term task gains alongside skill regression on later unaided work. We report the design and three-semester evaluation of a Socratic-scaffolded conversational AI assistant in an introductory programming course at a northern Taiwanese university. The system layers retrieval grounding to instructor materials, Socratic-by-default response prompting, and metacognitive interaction tracking using Bloom's taxonomy. A cross-cohort task-effectiveness study (pooled N = 82) found large pre-to-post gains (d = 1.20) replicated across cohorts, although the absence of a non-scaffolded control precludes causal attribution. A perception study (N = 203) showed positive usability, acceptance, and satisfaction (normalized means 75–79%), with no decay across semesters. An interaction-pattern study (N = 90) revealed the predicted effort signature: users judged the Socratic mode more effortful yet endorsed it for perceived depth of understanding. We discuss implications for designing assistants for skill-building rather than task completion.

documents.abstract: Abstract Artificial intelligence is transforming online information environments, amplifying both societal benefits and risks. This article argues that online platforms can be understood as multi‐agent systems (MAS) composed of humans, simulated users, adversarial agents, and defensive agents operating under platform‐level rules. In this MAS‐based framework, persuasion, trust, coordination, and governance interact to shape system‐level outcomes. To study these dynamics safely, we introduce a sandbox environment in which human participants, red bots, green bots, and blue bots can be observed under controlled conditions. Early experiences with the sandbox show that persuasive agents can be built with little effort, that current large language model (LLM) agents lack psychological realism, and that humans may struggle to distinguish malicious red bots from benign participants. The sandbox enables stakeholders to experience and evaluate trade‐offs in moderation, amplification, and intervention strategies. We outline a research agenda for improving agent validity, modelling advanced threats, and designing human–machine teams that support healthier, more resilient information environments.

documents.abstract: Abstract Introduction: Artificial intelligence-based clinical decision support systems (AI CDSS) have the potential to improve clinical decision-making and patient outcomes, yet their adoption remains limited. Prior research highlights trust in AI and concerns about professional autonomy as key barriers to implementation. While explainability and system integration may foster trust, they may simultaneously threaten professional identity and decision authority. At the same time, perceived usefulness has been identified as the central driver of technology acceptance, although it is shaped by autonomyrelated concerns, particularly among physicians. This study integrates two experimental investigations (1,2) to examine how AI-CDSS design features jointly influence trust, autonomy-related perceptions, and acceptance across patients and physicians. Methods: The analysis combines and compares findings from two vignette-based experimental studies. The first study (n = 292) employs a 2 × 2 × 2 factorial design manipulating AI explainability, workflow integration, and accountability to assess their effects on trust and professional identity threat among physicians. The second study consists of three experiments across patients (n = 209), potential future users (n = 1062), and physicians (n = 185), manipulating AI-CDSS system type (hybrid vs. autonomous) and recommendation risk (lifestyle vs. medical) (2 x 2 factorial design). Regression-based mediation and sequential mediation models (SPSS PROCESS Macro) were applied using bootstrapping procedures. Results: Results from the first study show that explainability and workflow integration significantly increase trust in AI-CDSS. At the same time, explainability and system-induced accountability increase perceived professional identity threat. Trust is negatively associated with identity threat and partially mediates the relationship between explainability and identity threat, indicating that trust can mitigate but not fully offset these concerns. Results from the second study demonstrate that perceived usefulness is the strongest predictor of intention to use among both patients, potential future users, and physicians. However, the underlying mechanisms differ. Patients and potential future users evaluate AI-CDSS primarily based on perceived usefulness, whereas physicians’ evaluations depend on professional autonomy preservation. For physicians, hybrid systems increase intention to use only indirectly through reduced professional autonomy concerns and increased perceived usefulness. High-risk medical recommendations consistently increase perceived or anticipated professional autonomy concerns across all groups but do not directly reduce perceived usefulness or intention to use. Conclusion: AI-CDSS acceptance is shaped by the interplay of trust, perceived usefulness, and professional autonomy-related concerns. Design features exhibit ambivalent effects, simultaneously enabling and constraining adoption. Successful implementation requires aligning system design with professional expectations, particularly by preserving physician decision authority while demonstrating clear clinical value.

documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) systems are increasingly embedded in decisions that affect health, employment, housing, justice, and social policy. Rather than neutral tools, they reflect the data on which they are trained, the objectives they optimize, and the contexts in which they operate, reinforcing and amplifying existing social inequalities. This paper addresses two interrelated questions: how can we detect bias across the AI lifecycle, and what technical and governance strategies can effectively mitigate it? Drawing on critical social science perspectives, empirical case studies from healthcare, housing, policing, and labor markets, and recent advances in fair machine learning (including causal debiasing, synthetic data generation, and fair representation learning), the paper develops a conceptual framework, grounded in sociological theories, spanning data collection, preprocessing, model training, deployment, and post-deployment monitoring. As an original contribution, the paper proposes two complementary analytical frameworks: a Social Harm-Intervention Mapping that recasts mitigation strategies in terms of the types of inequality they address, and an Accountability Matrix that maps agency and accountability gaps across social actors and pipeline stages. The paper argues that these frameworks provide social researchers and policymakers with more actionable guidance than conventional pipeline taxonomies because they foreground the social and institutional dimensions of AI-induced inequality rather than treating bias as a purely technical problem.
